the-physiology-of-crunch.core: Sustained crunch keeps the body in stress mode: elevated cortisol, poor sleep, impaired prefrontal function (judgement, focus, memory) and weakened immunity. Productivity per hour falls after ~50 hours a week, and error rates rise, which in operations means more incidents. Burnout is a physiological state, not a lack of willpower.

first_principles.problem: A team on 70-hour weeks ships more bugs than when they worked 40.
truths: Output per hour declines with long hours.

analogy.title: Running a car engine in the red
analogy.story: It goes faster for a while, then overheats and breaks down.
analogy.breaks: Engines can be replaced; recovering from burnout takes months.

example.title: Crunch cost
flow: Net delivery lower than a 45 h/week plan

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Crunch borrows from the future at high interest.

check.q: Name the three dimensions of burnout (Maslach).
check.a: Exhaustion, cynicism/depersonalisation and reduced professional efficacy.

passive-vs-active-recovery.core: Passive recovery (scrolling, TV) feels restful but often doesn't restore. Active recovery (exercise, time in nature, social connection, hobbies that absorb attention, sleep hygiene) rebuilds energy. Psychological detachment from work, relaxation, mastery experiences and control over free time are the evidence-based recovery ingredients.

first_principles.problem: An engineer spends every weekend on the sofa and still feels drained on Monday.
truths: Rest isn't the same as recovery.

analogy.title: Charging a phone versus just turning the screen off
analogy.story: Screen-off saves a little; plugging in actually recharges.
analogy.breaks: Phones charge predictably; human recovery varies by person and stress level.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Energy noticeably higher in two weeks.

check.a: Mentally switching off from work during time off: not thinking about or checking work.

the-right-to-disconnect.core: Always-on chat and on-call culture erode recovery. Set explicit boundaries: defined working hours, notification schedules, clear on-call rotations with compensation, and team norms that non-urgent messages wait. Several countries now legislate a 'right to disconnect'.

first_principles.problem: Engineers answer Slack at midnight because nobody knows what's expected.

analogy.title: Office doors with opening hours
analogy.story: The shop has hours, and an emergency number for real emergencies.
analogy.breaks: Shops close physically; digital work leaks unless norms are explicit.

check.q: Why should managers use scheduled send for late-night messages?
check.a: It avoids implying an expectation of immediate off-hours response.

re-entry-the-no-muscle.core: Returning from burnout, the risk is sliding back into the same overload. Build the 'no muscle': prioritise explicitly, say no or 'not now' with alternatives, negotiate scope instead of hours, and protect focus time. Saying no to low-value work is saying yes to high-value work and health.

first_principles.problem: After recovery leave, an engineer accepts every request again and is burnt out within months.
truths: Clear priorities make saying no easier.

analogy.title: A plate at a buffet
analogy.story: You can't take everything; choosing deliberately leaves room for what you really want.
analogy.breaks: Buffets are self-serve; work requests come from people you want to help, which makes no harder.

branches.label: Mindset
children: No to X = yes to Y

example.title: Saying no constructively
flow: Request: 'Can you lead the new migration too?'
'I'd like to help. If I take it, the observability project slips a month; which matters more?'

check.a: Agreeing to a request on the condition that something else is dropped or delayed, making the trade-off explicit.
